quote: Sind alle durch Lineal und Zirkel ausführ- baren Constructionen auch durch Zirkel allein ausführbar?
english: Can all constructions that can be carried out with ruler and compass also be carried out with compass alone?
topic: Three short notes: Minkowski's conjecture that a closed surface of flexible but inextensible material cannot be continuously bent (especially the sphere); whether all ruler-and-compass constructions can be done with compass alone; and a task to prove that no number in the cyclotomic field other than the root of unity has discriminant equal to the field discriminant.

triage.modern_statement: In the Euclidean plane, take any point that can be constructed from a given finite set of points with straightedge and compass. Can that same point also be constructed from the same set with a compass alone? A line counts as 'given' once two of its points are known, since a compass can't draw lines. Put another way: do compass-only constructions reach exactly the same points as straightedge-and-compass constructions?
triage.answered_by: Yes. This is the Mohr–Mascheroni theorem. Lorenzo Mascheroni proved it independently in 1797 ('Geometria del compasso'), and for a long time it was called Mascheroni's theorem. Georg Mohr had already proved it in 'Euclides Danicus' (1672), but that book was forgotten until it turned up in 1928. Johannes Hjelmslev then republished it in German translation with a foreword. So when Hilbert wrote the note, Mascheroni's answer was already known in the literature.

evidence.claim: The Mohr–Mascheroni theorem says any construction possible with compass and straightedge is possible with a compass alone. Mohr proved it in 1672 but his proof stayed obscure until 1928. Mascheroni found it independently in 1797, and it was called Mascheroni's Theorem until Mohr's work was rediscovered.

Mohr's 'Euclides danicus' (1672) contains a proof that all Euclidean constructions can be done with compasses alone. It was found in a bookstore in 1928, and J. Hjelmslev republished it in German with a foreword. Mascheroni's proof came 125 years after Mohr's.

triage.why: Hilbert's question is exactly what the Mohr–Mascheroni theorem answers, and the answer is yes. Mascheroni published it in 1797, about a century before this notebook entry, so the note reads as Hilbert raising or recalling a classical question rather than an open problem. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. It is a settled classical result. Related topics such as the compass equivalence theorem and Poncelet–Steiner constructions belong to classical geometry, and my sources don't show any active research on this question.
